subtype: Approach: talking to Indians already living there [Action]
passage:
Neelam had a shiny brochure from a consultancy and a lot of questions it did not answer. On a Sunday in her Mumbai flat, she wrote a short message and sent it to five professionals she found through an alumni group who lived in Toronto.
"I'm thinking of moving. Could you tell me what rent really costs, what tax takes, how long your job hunt took, and whether it gets lonely?"
By Wednesday four had replied. Rent was higher than the brochure said. One had needed five months to find a job. Abhinav wrote the longest note: the first winter was the hardest, and he had called home every night.
Neelam read them at the kitchen table, unsettled and grateful in equal measure, and made a fresh list of questions.

qa.q: How many professionals did Neelam message?
What was Neelam feeling as she read the replies?
qa.a: Neelam was unsettled and grateful at once, learning things the brochure had left out.

qa.q: What could Neelam do with the fresh list of questions?
qa.a: Neelam could ask the same people, and a few others, and compare their answers before making any decision.

qa.q: How might Abhinav have felt writing the longest note?
qa.a: Abhinav was probably remembering his hard first winter and wanted to be honest so that Neelam would be prepared.

grounding: The passage shows a person messaging five professionals in the target city about rent, taxes, job hunting time and loneliness to get a picture beyond brochures.

subtype: Approach: talking to Indians already living there [Action]
passage:
'Thanks for picking up, Reena. You're the third person I've asked. Can I ask the boring things?'
'Boring is good. Go.'
'Rent. Real rent, not the brochure.'
'For a one-bedroom near work, about half my take-home. Most people share for the first year.'
'Taxes?'
'Higher than at home. Use the official calculator, don't trust anyone's rough number, including mine.'
'How long did your job hunt take?'
'Five months, and I had a visa sponsor lined up. Friends without one took longer.'
'And... is it lonely?'
Reena laughed, then didn't. 'The first winter, yes. Very. I ate dinner on video calls with my mother for months.'
Sunaina wrote it all under 'Person 3' in her notebook. Two more calls to go before she would open any consultant's brochure again.

qa.q: How long did Reena's job hunt take?
qa.a: Five months, with a visa sponsor lined up.

qa.q: How does Sunaina seem to feel asking these questions?
qa.a: Sunaina seems a little shy and apologetic about the 'boring' questions, but determined to hear real costs instead of brochure promises.

qa.q: What else could Sunaina do with notes from all five people?
qa.a: Sunaina could compare the answers side by side and check the numbers on official sites, so the picture rests on more than one story.

qa.q: How might Reena see these questions?
qa.a: Reena seems glad to be asked plainly, and honest enough to admit the lonely first winter, something Reena may have wished to hear before moving.

grounding: It shows a person asking professionals in the target city about real rent, taxes, job-hunt time and loneliness rather than relying on brochures.

subtype: Approach: talking to Indians already living there [Action]
passage:
I'm Suraj, and before I spent a rupee on applications, I sent the same message to five people from my college who work in Melbourne: 'Can I ask you three honest questions for fifteen minutes?' Four said yes. Nitin, who graduated two years before me, called the same night.
I asked each of them the same things: what do you really pay in rent, how long did your first job take, and when did you feel lonely? The answers didn't match the consultancy brochure at all. Rent was nearly double what the brochure showed. Two had taken over six months to find work in their field. Nitin said the loneliness hit in month three and stayed until he joined a cricket club.
I'm still going. But I'm going with a budget and a plan for month three.

qa.q: How many people said yes to Suraj's message?
How does Suraj seem to feel about going, after the calls?
qa.a: Suraj feels more grounded and clear-eyed, still hopeful but prepared for the hard months instead of dazzled by a brochure.

qa.q: What else could Suraj add to the plan for month three?
qa.a: Suraj could look up clubs or community groups in Melbourne before leaving, as the cricket club helped Nitin.

qa.q: How might Nitin see being contacted by a junior?
qa.a: Nitin may feel glad to help and remember his own loneliness, which is perhaps why he called the same night.

grounding: It shows a person messaging professionals in the target city about real rent, job-hunt time and loneliness to see beyond the brochures.
